title: Vertical CCD strings: 3D NAND geometry clocked as charge-coupled DRAM
idea: Revive 1970s CCD serial memory inside a 3D-NAND-like stack: a vertical gate-all-around oxide-semiconductor or poly channel with 128 wordline tiers is clocked in three phases to shift charge packets up and down, with one sense/regenerate amplifier at the string foot. There is no per-cell contact, capacitor or access transistor, and bidirectional shifting halves average latency.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 7: cell area approaches 3D NAND bit density (~10x DRAM per mm2) and one sense amp serves 128 bits; ~60-130 ns access fits the DRAM-class window for streaming data.

title: Hourglass: pinched-waist vertical channel trims the leakage tail
idea: An hourglass narrows in the middle: shape each vertical access channel with a ~5 nm waist at the gate center (an oxidation-pinch step) and wide ends for low contact resistance, so the gate-drain edge field and the GIDL and trap-assisted leakage tail drop. The die skips most of the controller's REF commands internally while keeping DDR5 timing.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): 13 fA tail to ~2-3 fA; internal refresh rate 4x lower, refresh energy -50-75%.

title: Direct-tunneling hBN floating gate for van der Waals quasi-volatile tiers
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping (rush through the harmful stage): charge a graphene floating gate through a 3-layer hBN barrier by pure direct tunneling in ns, never entering the Fowler-Nordheim/hot-carrier regime that creates traps. The dangling-bond-free barrier keeps endurance DRAM-like with seconds of retention, and MoS2-channel tiers stack as transferred 2D films.
why: Fact 3: capacitorless 1T cell with ~100x longer retention than DRAM (refresh energy -99%) built in low-temperature tiers stackable on logic.

title: DVD replication: molded substrates carry all cell topography
idea: Adapted from DVD/Blu-ray replication (a nanostructured disc molded every ~3 s from one nickel stamper): mold glass-ceramic or high-Tg substrates that already contain capacitor wells, gate trenches and contact steps, then conformally coat electrode, high-k, IGZO and metal and planarize, so array geometry needs no lithography.
why: Collapses 5-7 EUV layers and their etches (fact 4) into one molding amortized over ~10^5 parts, ~100x lower patterning cost per GB; trade-offs: ~40 nm features, low-temperature materials, slower cells.

title: Vertical-bitline triple-tier activation computes majority inside stack
idea: Inverts 'tiers are independent storage whose data must leave the stack.' Open three tiers on a shared vertical bitline at once so charge sharing yields bitwise majority, and copy between tiers by one vertical charge share, so whole-pillar AND/OR/copy/zero never crosses the I/O.
why: Fact 5: bulk operations move zero bits off-stack; ~10-100x energy cut for memset, copy and bitmap workloads.

title: Infrared through-silicon optical links replace Bosch-etched copper TSVs
idea: Substitute SF6/C4F8 Bosch-etched Cu TSVs with vertical free-space optics: silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so beams from bonded InP micro-emitters (Cl2/BCl3-etched) on the base die cross 30 um-thin DRAM dies to Ge-on-Si detectors (GeH4 epi) placed at a unique XY site on each die (position multiplexing).
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no via keep-out zones or via yield loss, which drive much of the 3x area per bit, and the stack is built with no fluorinated deep-etch gases.

title: Multi-height imprint stamp encodes all cell layers, zero web overlay
idea: Imprint one resist layer with a 4-5 level stamp whose heights encode gate, channel, via and capacitor patterns, then pattern each layer by successive etch-backs that expose the next height, so every level is self-aligned by the stamp itself.
why: First principles: PET expands ~20 ppm/C, so 1 C across a 30 cm web is ~6 um of misregistration, making overlay the true R2R density limit; encoding overlay in the stamp enables sub-um cells with one stamp instead of a mask set (fact 4).

title: Oxygen pinch-off of Bosch scallops yields stacked nanowire tiers
idea: Etch tall Si fins with a deliberately scalloped Bosch (SF6/C4F8) cycle, then dry-oxidize at ~1000 C so the narrow necks between scallops oxidize through first, leaving vertically stacked, oxide-isolated horizontal Si nanowires, one per scallop, as lateral access-transistor tiers.
why: Crystalline stacked lateral channels (fact 2) from bulk Si using only DRIE and a furnace; scallop period sets tier pitch (~100-200 nm) for 4-10-tier university demonstrations.

title: Anodic alumina pores self-assemble litho-free 3D cell arrays
idea: Revive the 1950s Keller anodic aluminum oxide pore process used in electrolytic capacitors: anodize thick aluminum into self-ordered ~25-40 nm pitch vertical pores that template capacitor and channel pillars without lithography, accepting ~1% irregular or merged pores as failed cells.
why: Fact 4: removes EUV/immersion litho layers from the cell array, cutting capital per bit with abundant aluminum.

title: Every vertical bitline bonded down to its own generous sense amp
idea: Po: the sense amp is bigger than the cells it serves. Fabricate only arrays on a litho-light 'array wafer' with vertical bitlines spanning 64+ tiers, and all sense amps and decoders on a separate logic wafer, hybrid-bonded at ~0.5 um pitch so each bond carries one vertical bitline to a large, low-offset sense amp.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and capital: array fab drops logic-transistor steps (~30% fewer masks); larger matched sense amps (offset <5 mV) let Cs shrink, easing the charge wall.

title: Logic-heat-biased VO2 hysteresis latches in BEOL tiers
idea: Thermal hysteresis: VO2 nano-bridge cross-point tiers are placed on the logic die, whose steady ~60-65 C waste heat parks every bridge inside its doped, widened hysteresis window. A heat pulse sets a bridge metallic, and a small hold bias keeps it there by self-heating. Briefly removing a row's bias resets that row before selective re-set.
why: Turns stacking heat, normally a refresh penalty (fact 3), into the storage bias; claim a capacitor-free BEOL latch at ~4F2 per tier with no refresh.

title: Fermented S-layer protein crystals as sub-10 nm cell masks
idea: Grow bacterial surface-layer (S-layer) proteins by fermentation; they self-crystallize on wafers into 2D lattices of 10-20 nm period, which are metallized or infiltrated into a hard mask that defines vertical-channel or capacitor arrays without EUV.
why: Replaces 5-7 EUV array layers (fact 4) with a bioreactor product costing cents per wafer; defects handled by redundancy mapping; long-range order and registration to periphery are the risk.

title: Fiber-draw nanocapillary scaffold grown on a draw tower, not etched
idea: Use the optical-fiber draw tower: stack a centimetre preform of glass rods with soluble cores, draw it down ~10,000x into a fused bundle with ~40 nm channels and >1000:1 aspect ratio, slice 3 um wafers, bond them onto the transistor wafer, and ALD electrodes plus high-k into the channels to form the capacitor forest.
why: Capacitor wall and etch capital (facts 1, 4): AR far beyond the 115 target with zero deep plasma etch; replaces cryogenic high-AR etch tools with draw towers costing a few $M.

title: N-type-only IGZO sense latches built inside every 3D tier
idea: [Box: lateral 1T1C | IGZO access | nMOS-only bootstrapped dynamic latch | monolithic BEOL tiers | Si | ALD IGZO] Rather than hauling every tier's bitline down to CMOS under the array, build a compact n-only cross-coupled latch (precharge-evaluate with bootstrap capacitors) from the same IGZO in each tier, sensing short local bitlines and driving amplified full-swing data onto a global line.
why: Charge-share ratio (fact 1) and under-array periphery limits (fact 7): 4-8x shorter local bitlines let Cs fall to ~2 fF, removing the need for high-AR capacitors.

title: Sky-lobby decoder decks: in-stack tier decoders fed by express vias
idea: Skyscrapers use express elevators to sky lobbies, then local cars; build a 128-tier 3D DRAM as 8 decks of 16 tiers, each deck capped by a thin-film decoder tier that receives a 4-bit tier address over a few express vias and fans out locally to its 16 wordline planes through a short mini-staircase.
why: 3D staircase and periphery (facts 2, 7): wires from the CMOS base drop from one per tier to ~log2 per deck, shrinking the staircase/contact region ~4-8x and letting tier count rise without periphery growth.

title: Core-memory coincident selection for 3D tier addressing without staircases
idea: Ferrite core memory died on hand-threading labor, but its coincident-current X-Y selection was elegant. Make each 3D DRAM access transistor dual-gated, one gate on a horizontal tier plane and one on a vertical pillar gate, so a cell turns on only when both are driven. N planes by M pillars then select any cell with N+M drivers instead of a staircase and decoder per tier.
why: Removes staircase contact area and periphery growth in 3D DRAM (facts 2, 7). Decoder count grows with the square root of cell count instead of linearly.

title: Burn-out amorphous-carbon tiers replace nitride sacrificial layers in 3D
idea: Substitute sacrificial nitride/oxide tiers with PECVD amorphous-carbon tiers alternating with Si or IGZO channel tiers: cut slits with Cl2 (channel) and O2 (carbon), keep support pillars every ~2 um, then laterally ash the carbon with remote O2/H2 plasma (selectivity >1000:1) to open horizontal cavities for lateral capacitors.
why: Solves the lateral-capacitor cavity step of 3D DRAM (fact 2) with a dry release needing no HF or NF3; propylene-derived carbon is cheap and non-scarce.

title: Temperature-proofed T-RAM: vertical thyristor pillars with PTAT-tracked gate
idea: T-RAM (thyristor RAM) was dropped because its latch hold current and blocking voltage drifted strongly with temperature, causing standby leakage and fails at 85C. Build a 4F2 vertical p-n-p-n pillar with a gated base, driving the gate from an on-die PTAT (proportional-to-absolute-temperature) reference in each bank so latch current stays constant from -40 to 125C. Latched cells need no refresh and no capacitor.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3: 16-33% of idle power) and the capacitor (fact 1) in a 4F2 footprint (fact 4). Claims about 1.5x density vs 6F2 and near-zero refresh energy.

title: Backside-illuminated sensor thinning fused with double-sided trench DRAM
idea: Reuse the CMOS-image-sensor flow at a US 300 mm fab (onsemi East Fishkill, the old IBM trench-DRAM site): etch full-depth deep-trench capacitors, thin the wafer to ~3 um as in BSI sensors, and contact capacitor plates and power from the backside while access transistors and bitlines own the front.
why: Facts 1 and 7: plate/strap contacts and power leave the front side (~20% tighter cell pitch); trench depth is fixed by thinning rather than etch AR; revives domestic trench know-how for a capital-light line.

title: Image-sensor pixel bonding: one sense amp per 64 cells
idea: Borrowed from stacked CMOS image sensors with pixel-level Cu-Cu hybrid bonds and per-pixel ADCs: bond the array wafer face-to-face to a logic wafer at sub-1 um pitch so every 64-cell micro-bitline lands on its own sense amp, eliminating long bitlines entirely.
why: Bitline capacitance falls from ~50-80 fF to ~2 fF, so Cs can drop to ~0.5 fF (no 70:1 pillar, fact 1), read energy ~10x lower, and periphery leaves the array die (fact 7).

title: Image-sensor ramp ADCs read sixteen charge levels per cell
idea: Borrowed from CMOS image sensors, whose column-parallel single-slope ADCs digitize thousands of pixels with one shared ramp: each bitline gets a tiny comparator-counter so a cell holds 16 charge levels (4 bits), written by ramp-and-stop and digitally restored on every read.
why: 4 bits/cell lets a 40 nm ArF-dry, EUV-free array at ~1/5 the wafer cost match today's density; with 16 stacked tiers cost per GB falls ~100x; trade-offs: ~200 ns reads, more frequent refresh.

title: Astronomer's bucket brigade: CCD charge chains instead of capacitor cells
idea: An astronomer stores charge in CCD potential wells and reads single electrons at one output amplifier. Build 8-stage buried-channel charge-coupled chains in a 22-40 nm image-sensor foundry, via MPW. Each bit is ~100 electrons under one gate with no contact or capacitor, and a floating-diffusion amplifier serves every 8 bits.
why: Removes capacitor, cell contacts and most sense amps. CCD dark current gives seconds of retention (Facts 1, 3, 7), and the whole thing is made in a US/Israel CIS foundry with a fabless 10-person team.

title: Goto-pair Esaki tunnel latch stacked in one vertical pillar
idea: Interband tunneling (negative differential resistance): two series Si/SiGe Esaki tunnel diodes, grown epitaxially in one vertical pillar, form a bistable Goto-pair storage node. A single surrounding access gate connects that node to the bitline. The result is a static, capacitor-free 4F2 cell held by pA-level tunnel current.
why: Removes both the capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3); claim 4F2 static density at a few nW per Mb standby, with no refresh bandwidth loss.

title: Bank-per-tile memory: DRAM bank footprint equals one compute tile
idea: IFR: 'every operand already sits on top of its ALU.' Backward: lay out a DRAM wafer whose bank grid exactly matches the accelerator's tile grid and face-to-face hybrid-bond it, each bank with a private ~4,000-bond vertical port, so a tile reads only its own bank across ~5 um.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, a 10-30x cut in memory I/O energy.

title: Two-mask array: hole-and-slit concentric annular 3D DRAM cells
idea: Limit: the whole array may use only two critical masks. One hole mask through 96 Si/SiGe tiers defines vertical bitlines, and a timed lateral recess from each hole carves a concentric ring per tier (BL core, then an annular channel gated by the tier plates above and below, then an outer ring capacitor). One slit mask cuts the plates into wordline regions, so a cell is the crossing of one hole and one tier-region.
why: Facts 2 and 4: about 10,000 nm2 per tier-cell at 100 nm hole pitch gives about 104 nm2/bit over 96 tiers (8x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV array layers.

title: Minify bitline to 16 cells with 2-transistor local preamp
idea: Cut each bitline into 16-cell segments. Each segment drives a global bitline through a 2-transistor local preamplifier, so the bitline capacitance seen by a cell falls from about 80 fF to about 3 fF. With that ratio, Cs can shrink from 5 fF to about 0.5 fF, and the capacitor becomes a shallow planar or low-AR cup instead of a 70:1 pillar.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Cs needed drops by 10x, removing the need for AR 115 or k 70. Area overhead is about 12%, against much cheaper capacitor process steps.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM with defect-routing mesh bonded to accelerators
idea: Leave a 300 mm DRAM wafer undiced, link its ~2,000 mats through a redundant on-wafer mesh that test maps around bad mats, and wafer-to-wafer bond it face-to-face to an accelerator wafer so every compute tile has DRAM within millimetres.
why: Data movement (fact 5): wire energy scales with distance, so going from mm-to-cm package traces to um bond pads drops ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, and dicing, packaging, interposers and TSVs disappear.

title: Retention-tiered monolithic stack with minutes-retention tiers for KV data
idea: Serve the AI KV-cache user whose data lives seconds to minutes: in one monolithic 3D stack the lower tiers use a thicker tunnel barrier around a charge-storage gate (minutes retention, slower write) while the top tiers keep fast capacitor cells, and the controller places each KV block by expected lifetime. The tier recipes differ in a single dielectric thickness, so it remains one process flow.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) vanishes for the long-lived bulk of KV data and capacitor-free tiers are denser (fact 1); ~2-4x capacity per die at similar cost.

title: Titanium dioxide rutile on fluorine-tin-oxide electrodes for compact lateral capacitors
idea: Use conductive F-doped SnO2 (rutile structure, ALD at ~250 C) as the storage-node electrode so ALD TiO2 nucleates directly as rutile (k ~80-100) instead of anatase (k ~30), replacing Ru-templated stacks; 1% Al doping plus a thin Al2O3 interlayer hold leakage.
why: Delivers the k ~70+ the charge wall needs (fact 1), so lateral 3D-DRAM capacitors shrink to short cups inside a tier instead of 60-75:1 pillars, using only Sn, Ti, F and O.

title: Row-hammer adversary design: tier-interleaved rows with grounded shield planes
idea: Design for a malicious user who hammers rows: map logically adjacent rows onto different tiers of a 3D array and insert grounded metal shield planes between tiers, so no aggressor shares a tier or electrostatic coupling path with its logical neighbors. The memory controller's address hash enforces the tier interleave.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): coupling-driven flips pushed from ~1k toward >100k activations, removing TRR/RFM overhead (~5-10% bandwidth) and the attack surface.

title: Three-way road junction: sense amps shared by three hexagonal mats
idea: Forced connection from a three-way junction: tile the die with hexagonal mats so each sense-amp cluster sits where three mats meet, and multiplex one sense amp across bitlines from three mats instead of the two of open-bitline sharing. Sub-wordline drivers line the hex edges and serve the two mats on either side.
why: Periphery is 49% of the die (fact 7): one-third fewer sense amps per bit; claim periphery ~49% to ~40% of the die and ~15% more bits per wafer.

title: Diffraction-grating interference lithography patterns periodic arrays maskless
idea: Adapted from holographic diffraction-grating production: since cell arrays are periodic, expose the whole array with two- or three-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~40 nm half-pitch, no mask, no EUV) and use cheap conventional litho only for array edges and periphery.
why: Interference tools cost ~1/20 of a scanner and expose a wafer in seconds; combined with 3D tiers, patterning cost per bit ~-95% (fact 4) toward 100x per GB.

title: Ship in a bottle: cell wafer bonded onto 28nm periphery wafer
idea: Build the ship outside, then slide it in: make a cell-only wafer (arrays, bitline sense amps and local column mux in the cell process) and a separate periphery wafer in a mature 28 nm logic fab carrying decoders, data paths and the standard DDR5 PHY, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond at ~0.5 um pitch with one bond per 16 bitlines. The bonded die is a normal DDR5 x8 part with the same pinout, commands and timing.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and EUV capital (fact 4): cell-wafer area per bit about -40%, and periphery moves to depreciated U.S. 28 nm fabs (U.S. manufacturability).

title: Nantero lesson: quarantine exotic memory films on a bonded wafer
idea: Nantero's carbon-nanotube NRAM stalled partly because fabs would not let CNT material into front-end lines for fear of contamination. Make the exotic memory film (CNT, chalcogenide or any new material) on a separate carrier wafer in a small dedicated US line, then hybrid-bond it onto the finished CMOS periphery wafer, so the CMOS fab never touches the material.
why: Breaks the fab-acceptance barrier that kills new cells (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability): new memory layers in a $200-500M line instead of a $15B fab.

title: Antiferroelectric-ferroelectric bilayer capacitor parks idle rows nonvolatilely
idea: Stack antiferroelectric ZrO2 (linear-like, unlimited-endurance charge storage) with a thin ferroelectric HZO in one capacitor: active banks store bits as AFE charge, and when a bank idles the controller 'parks' each row into FE polarization, stopping refresh until the next access.
why: Refresh (fact 3): idle-bank refresh power (16-33% of idle) to ~0; FE layer switches only on park/unpark (~10^6 cycles per day budget).

title: Built-in-bias antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitors stacked in 1T-nC strings
idea: Field-induced antiferroelectric-ferroelectric transition: ZrO2 capacitors with asymmetric-workfunction electrodes shift the double hysteresis loop so one lobe straddles zero bias, giving two non-volatile states. Antiferroelectric switching fatigues less than true ferroelectrics. Several such capacitors are stacked vertically on one access transistor.
why: Gives non-volatile, high-endurance stacked bits (facts 1 and 2) with n bits per transistor; claim 4-8 bits per access device and >1e12 cycles.

title: Tardigrade tun-state: data compacts into wide-bandgap tiers when hot
idea: Tardigrades survive heat by contracting into a dormant tun; build a hybrid stack with a few high-retention oxide-semiconductor gain-cell tiers above dense Si tiers, and when the on-die sensor passes ~105 C the controller compacts cold pages into the oxide tiers (seconds of retention even at 125 C) and stops refreshing those pages' Si homes.
why: At 125 C refresh would eat 30-50% of bandwidth; tun migration bounds refresh overhead at temperature while keeping full density at normal temperatures.

title: Fiber-drawn memory: thermally draw a cm-scale array preform 1000x smaller
idea: Shrink with a drawing tower instead of a stepper: assemble a cm-scale preform of chalcogenide-glass semiconductor, polymer dielectric and low-melting metal electrodes in a cell-array cross-section, and draw it down 1000-10000x to nm features. Slice and bundle the fiber cross-sections into tiles bonded to 180-nm CMOS periphery.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): patterning by deformation instead of litho; a fiber tower costs ~$1M against ~$200M for EUV, and features shrink with the draw ratio.

title: Self-referencing double read cancels printed transistor threshold scatter
idea: Read each printed cell, write a known '1', read again through the same bitline and sense amp, compare the two samples, then restore the original data, so the cell's own capacitor and TFT threshold become its reference.
why: Printed TFT Vt scatter (~100-300 mV) and +/-20% capacitor variation would collapse a fixed-reference sense margin; self-reference turns cell variation into common mode, tolerating ~10x worse variability at ~2x read time (~40-60 ns).

title: Capillary self-alignment for cheap high-throughput die-to-wafer stacking
idea: Surface tension: hydrophilic bond pads with hydrophobic surroundings, plus a water microdroplet, pull each roughly placed die to <200 nm alignment as the water evaporates, before direct hybrid bonding. Fast, coarse pick-and-place replaces slow precision bonders.
why: Cuts capital and throughput limits of HBM and 3D die stacking (facts 4 and 6); claim 5-10x die-to-wafer throughput per tool, which suits US assembly lines.

title: Antiferroelectric imprint crosspoint revives Bell's 1952 BaTiO3 matrix memory
idea: Bell Labs' 1952 passive BaTiO3 crosspoint memory died from half-select disturb; revive it with imprint-shifted, ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO whose double hysteresis loop gives a sharp switching threshold that V/3 half-select cannot reach, stacking 8 selectorless decks of 20 nm lines at <=400 C.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: effective ~0.5F2 per bit with no transistor or capacitor tower; AFE cycling (>1e12) plus wear leveling approaches DRAM endurance needs.

title: Atanasoff capacitor-drum brushes: sense amps commutated across mats
idea: Revive the Atanasoff-Berry Computer's capacitor drum, where a few brushes served thousands of capacitors: mats carry no local sense amps, and a small pool of sense amps is commutated across 8 mats through a low-capacitance charge-transfer bitline multiplexer that pre-amplifies before switching.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp count and pitch-matched area shrink ~8x, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% at a modest bank-parallelism cost.

title: Eliminate electrical wordlines: optically gated photo-TFT access
idea: Replace metal wordlines and their 3 V drivers with a row-scanning micro-LED or waveguide grating that illuminates one row of photoconductive oxide-semiconductor access switches; dark switches have very low leakage, while lit ones conduct.
why: Voltage floor: the ~3 V wordline swing and its CV2 energy disappear, and row hammer from wordline coupling vanishes; switching speed is the open risk.

title: Pillar-first stacking: grow tall nanowire bitlines, then deposit tiers
idea: Worse: drill ever-deeper holes through a finished tier stack until etch aspect ratio caps tier count. Flip: grow the vertical bitline/channel pillars FIRST by templated selective-area epitaxy (bottom-up AR >100 is routine for nanowires), then build the tiers around them with conformal deposition and one blanket CMP per tier, so stack height comes from growth and deposition and no deep etch ever happens.
why: Removes the high-AR etch that blocks manufacturable 3D DRAM (facts 2, 4); tier count no longer capped near 75:1, plausibly 150+ tiers with zero per-tier lithography.

title: Eliminate wafer slicing and polishing: dry spalled kerfless donor films
idea: Peel 20-50 um silicon films from an ingot face by controlled spalling with a sputtered stressor layer instead of wire-sawing, lapping and polishing wafers, and use the films as thin tier donors for stacked arrays.
why: Water and scarce resource: wafering's slurry, saw coolant and polish rinses vanish, and kerf loss goes to zero, so ingots (and quartz crucibles) per bit drop ~2x and wafering water >10x.

title: Band-offset quantum-well bits stacked along a superlattice pillar
idea: Worse: store each bit on a bulky capacitor needing femtofarads. Flip: etch vertical pillars through a Si/Ge-rich superlattice, wrap each Ge-rich well with a tier gate, and store holes in its valence-band well (up to ~0.5 eV offset) as the bit, sensed as a threshold shift of the shared vertical Si channel, which is capacitorless and has no oxide tunneling, so endurance stays unlimited.
why: Every tier of every pillar is a bit: 128 tiers at 50 nm pillar pitch is ~17 nm2/bit (~50x), so 10x survives even at 20% array efficiency with NAND-like process cost; retention from thermal emission over the band offset is the speculative part.

title: Printed liquid-silane ink laser-crystallized into polysilicon periphery
idea: Print cyclopentasilane ink only for decoder, wordline-driver and sense circuits, convert it to amorphous silicon and excimer-laser crystallize it to ~100 cm^2/Vs polysilicon, while the cell access devices stay wide-gap oxide.
why: Drive current scales with mobility, so periphery runs ~10x faster than oxide TFTs, letting a fully printed foil reach ~20-50 ns access; it also avoids Czochralski wafers and their Spruce Pine quartz-crucible chokepoint.

title: Amplifier tiers interleaved every eight storage tiers
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: every 9th tier of the 3D stack is built from the same lateral transistors but wired as single-ended pre-amplifiers (gated source followers). Each one buffers an 8-tier local vertical bitline segment before it drives the long global bitline to the sense amp below.
why: Fact 1 and 2: cell needs ~1/4 the charge because the local segment capacitance is tiny, so lateral capacitors can be short and thin, making 26+ tiers practical.

title: Plate wordlines and hole bitlines: one-mask annular 3D DRAM
idea: [Box: annular lateral capacitor | annular IGZO channel | charge-share SA | 3D-NAND-like plate stack | Si | blanket stack + one ArF hole mask + isotropic recesses] Each tier is a blanket wordline plate; one hole etch through all tiers forms vertical bitlines, and isotropic recesses carve an annular IGZO channel and ring capacitor around every hole in every tier, so a cell is (tier, hole) and mask count is independent of tier count.
why: No EUV + 3D (facts 2, 4): ArF holes at ~80 nm pitch x 100 tiers give ~64 nm2 per bit, ~13x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm; small ring Cs is the risk.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobbies: express vertical lines to zone decoders every 16 tiers
idea: Copy high-rise elevator design: split a 256-tier stack into 16-tier zones, run a few express vertical lines to a lobby tier in each zone that holds thin-film local decoders, and limit each zone's staircase to 16 steps. Contact area then grows with the log of tier count instead of linearly.
why: Staircase and wordline-contact area grow with tier count and erode 3D density (facts 2, 7); claim a ~5-10x smaller staircase footprint at 256 tiers.

title: Twist vertical bitline pairs mid-stack for folded-pair noise cancellation
idea: Pair adjacent vertical bitline pillars as true/complement and swap their positions halfway up the stack through a crossover in a middle tier, so each sees equal coupling from every neighbor and the bottom sense amp gets a common-mode-free differential signal, restoring folded-bitline immunity in 3D.
why: Sense margin in 3D/open-bitline arrays (facts 1,2): 30-50% more usable margin allows ~30% smaller Cs or longer bitlines.

title: LIGO-style differential cell: true and complement capacitors stacked vertically
idea: Ultra-low-noise instruments sense differentially; store each bit as true and complement charge on two capacitors stacked one above the other in the same 4F2 footprint, a bottom-tier and a top-tier transistor sharing one vertical pillar, read by a reference-free differential amplifier. Signal doubles and reference and offset noise cancel, so each capacitor can be half the size.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): each capacitor ~2.5 fF at about half the aspect ratio (~35:1), easing the hardest etch while footprint density holds; immune to reference drift.

title: Periphery wafer sandwiched between two array wafers, cross-face sensing
idea: [Box: 1T1C | VCT | open-bitline SA with true line above and complement below | front hybrid bond + backside bond | thinned periphery Si | hybrid bonding + nano-TSV backside contacts] Bond one array wafer to the periphery wafer's front and another to its thinned backside, so every sense amp serves an open bitline from the top array and its complement from the bottom array.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): one periphery layer per two arrays halves periphery cost per bit, and balanced top/bottom pairs cancel array noise.

title: Rocket regenerative cooling: microchannels between bonded tiers allow 32-high
idea: Rocket nozzles survive by pumping coolant through channels in their own walls; wet-etch (TMAH, no plasma) 20 um microchannels into the backside of every fourth thinned DRAM die and bond with nitrogen-plasma-activated oxide instead of argon activation, so dielectric coolant flows through the stack and pulls heat from inside. Stacks grow to 24-32 high while staying below 85 C.
why: Layer count is thermally limited: cooler DRAM cuts refresh 2-4x (fact 3) and doubles capacity per stack, with argon-free bond activation.

title: Gain cell split across tiers: IGZO write above, silicon read below
idea: [Box: storage-node gate | IGZO write FET + Si read FET | current sense | sequential BEOL over FEOL | Si | ALD IGZO over 28 nm CMOS] Put the ultra-low-leakage IGZO write transistor in a BEOL tier directly over a high-drive Si read transistor in the substrate, with the vertical via between them as the storage node, giving each cell IGZO retention and Si read current in ~4-6F2.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and capacitor wall (fact 1): retention >1 s, no capacitor, Si-speed read; refresh energy down ~10x.

title: Transfluxor-inspired split-electrode ferroelectric cell with non-destructive read
idea: Revive the transfluxor, where the flux state around a major aperture blocked or freed switching around a minor one: a vertical ferroelectric capacitor has a large write electrode and a small adjacent read electrode, and the stored major domain's depolarizing field biases the minor region. Reading toggles only the minor region, which springs back, sensing state without disturbing the stored domain.
why: Fact 8: non-destructive read removes write-back energy and read fatigue; ~3-5x lower read energy, and ferroelectric endurance is spent only on real writes.

title: Multi-tier porous-oxide isolation: one bath makes 150 SOI tiers
idea: Worse: get single-crystal channels in every tier by bonding 150 wafers or by fragile SiGe replacement. Flip: grow a p+/p- doping superlattice of single-crystal Si, then electrochemically anodize from the slits so only the p+ layers turn porous, and thermally oxidize the porous layers into insulator, leaving 150 single-crystal Si-on-insulator tiers from one wet step.
why: Crystalline low-leakage channels in all tiers (fact 3) for one anodize+oxidize step instead of per-tier bonding, keeping a 150-tier, 10x-density stack within today's wafer cost.

title: Leaf-vein looped wordline mesh survives broken staircase contacts
idea: Copy reticulate leaf venation, where loops reroute flow around damage: tie each tier's wordline plate to its driver through a looped mesh of 3-4 staircase contacts with distributed straps, so an open contact or cracked stair reroutes current through neighbouring loops instead of killing the tier.
why: 3D yield versus layer count: tier-killing contact defects drop by orders of magnitude, enabling >100 tiers without exponential yield loss.

title: Minify transferred tier to 30 nm: ion-cut two-tier 1T1C
idea: Use vendor Smart Cut SOI services to bond and transfer a 30 nm single-crystal Si film onto a first finished cell tier, then build the second tier below 450 C with laser anneal in a university fab, proving 2-tier monolithic 1T1C for about $500k.
why: 3D integration: single-crystal tiers, with better leakage than poly or oxide channels, and no per-tier wafer bonding at cell pitch.

title: Leaf veins: backside copper grid straps wordlines, halving driver stripes
idea: Leaf veins feed every cell through branching: after thinning, add a low-resistance backside Cu grid that straps each Ru or Mo wordline every 64 cells through nano-vias, so wordlines can be 4x longer at the same RC. The die needs fewer, larger sub-wordline driver stripes, and DDR5 tRCD is unchanged.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): sub-wordline driver area -50 to -75%, die about -8%; moving off tungsten wordlines also eases the China ~80% tungsten chokepoint.

title: IBM trench capacitor revived from the wafer backside
idea: Trench DRAM (IBM, Infineon, Qimonda) lost to stacked capacitors because a deep trench competes with the transistor for front-side area. After building 4F2 vertical transistors on the front, thin the wafer and deep-etch (DRIE) trenches from the backside directly under each pillar's source. Trench depth is then limited by the 5-10 um wafer thickness rather than by front-side topology.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1). The backside trench is equivalent to AR >150 and gives Cs >10 fF without a k~70 dielectric, while the front side stays free for 4F2 cells.

title: FeCl3-intercalated graphene buried wordlines replace tungsten
idea: Inverts 'buried wordlines are tungsten.' Grow multilayer graphene in the wordline trench by plasma CVD and intercalate FeCl3 to bring resistivity to a few uOhm-cm, competitive with size-degraded W at 10 nm widths, using only C, Fe and Cl.
why: W chokepoint (China ~80%) and fact 10: removes W from the array; graphene's tunable work function may also lower gate-induced drain leakage.

title: Tier-wide buried back-gate plane pulsed negative during retention
idea: Deposit a continuous conductive back-gate plane under each tier's lateral access-transistor layer; during idle a charge pump holds it near -1 V, raising every access transistor's Vt through body coupling, and returns only the tier being accessed to 0 V.
why: Leakage physics: subthreshold current falls one decade per ~70 mV of Vt, so a ~300 mV coupled shift gives ~4 decades lower tail leakage (fact 3), stretching refresh from 64 ms toward minutes and removing most of the 16-33% idle refresh power; the plane costs one deposition per tier, not area.

title: Eliminate the row decoder: token-ring sequential wordlines for weights
idea: For AI weight memory that is read in fixed order, replace random row decoders with a shift-register token chain along the mat edge that activates wordline n+1 after n; random access falls back to a small seek-and-stream jump table per bank.
why: Periphery ~49% of die: row decode/predecode area and energy drop by most of their share, giving ~10-15% die area and lower activation energy for streaming workloads.

title: Thermally drawn nanochannel glass slices replace etched capacitor holes
idea: Substitute etched holes with drawn glass: bundle acid-soluble core rods in an acid-resistant matrix glass, redraw 3-4 times to 30-50 nm channels (microchannel-plate style), fuse, saw into 10-20 um slices, leach cores in HCl, CMP with silica/KOH slurry, ALD electrodes, and oxide-bond the slice onto the transistor wafer using the channel-smaller-than-pad-gap landing rule.
why: Capacitor charge wall: AR set by slice thickness (300-500:1 possible) -> Cs >15 fF or smaller cells; capital shifts from EUV/HAR etch to glass draw towers, fully fluorine-free.

title: Persistent-photoconductivity oxide tiers written by through-stack light
idea: Persistent photoconductivity: a UV pulse sent down a vertical light pipe ionizes oxygen vacancies in IGZO/ZnO channel tiers into metastable donors that keep the channel conductive with the power off. A gate bias selects which tier captures the charge, and a positive-gate pulse erases by re-neutralizing the vacancies.
why: Gives non-volatile tiers with no capacitor and no per-tier write drivers (facts 1 and 7); claim days-to-months retention from a single light pipe per column, with the speed-retention trade as the risk.

title: Tailor's marker nesting: shape dies to harvest wafer-edge silicon
idea: Garment cutters nest pattern pieces to minimize scrap; design mature-node memory as small self-contained hexagonal banks that plasma dicing can cut in any outline, so partial wafer-edge regions yield sellable small dies.
why: Recovers ~5-10% more bits per wafer from existing capacity with zero new fab, raising usable supply.

title: Zamboni: in-array microheater lines anneal leaky cells during self-refresh
idea: A Zamboni resurfaces the ice between periods: thread thin TiN heater lines under each mat, and during self-refresh or idle copy a mat's data to a neighbor, pulse the mat to ~150-200 C for milliseconds to de-trap the interface charges behind variable-retention and leakage-tail cells, then copy it back. The controller never sees it and keeps issuing normal REF commands.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): pruning the 13 fA tail 3-5x lets the die skip internal refreshes, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and idle power by 10-20%.

title: Replacement capacitor: 200 placeholders swapped for high-k through the slit
idea: Worse: finish each tier's capacitor before building the next, so early tiers suffer every later anneal and every tier pays its own dielectric step. Flip: leave a sacrificial SiN placeholder at each tier's capacitor site, complete the whole stack, then through the slits exhume all placeholders and deposit electrode, high-k and plate into all 200 tiers in one ALD sequence, like NAND gate replacement.
why: Capacitor cost becomes ~O(1) in tier count and thermal budget stops accumulating (facts 1, 2), letting ~200 tiers reach 10x at near-2D wafer cost.

title: Sixteen-tier decks hybrid-bonded with stitched vertical bitlines
idea: IFR: 'unlimited tiers without an unlimited etch.' Backward: build 16-tier decks with modest 30:1 etches, thin each deck to ~3 um, and hybrid-bond decks face-to-back at ~200 nm pitch so each vertical bitline continues through bond pads; six bonds give 96 tiers.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): avoids 100:1+ etches for high tier counts and lets each deck pass known-good test before stacking.

title: Bond-interface dielectric turns facing pads into storage capacitors
idea: Po: the glue is the memory. Bond two wafers through a 4 nm ZrO2/Al2O3 laminate deposited on the facing Cu pads, so each pad pair becomes a MIM capacitor (~5-7 fF at 400 nm pitch); the top wafer holds access transistors and the bottom a common plate plus periphery.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: a 28 nm-class fab gets DRAM with no capacitor module or high-AR etch at all, for low-cost capacity and embedded memory (larger cell, far cheaper flow).

title: Graded-thickness tiers pre-compensate etch taper in deep 3D stacks
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: model the vertical hole's taper before deposition and grade each tier's Si/SiGe (or oxide) thickness so tiers near the narrow bottom are thicker. Lateral channel width and capacitor area then stay matched (Ion and Cs within ~3%) across 100+ tiers from a single etch.
why: Fact 2: ~2x tiers per single-deck etch instead of multi-deck stacking, saving a full deck of masks/etch/alignment per ~64 tiers and tightening the retention tail.

title: Roll-to-roll memory book: one hundred laminated oxide-TFT foils
idea: Print-shop analogy: produce oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays roll-to-roll on 5 um polyimide or steel foil, cut sheets, and laminate 100 of them into a book whose spine is edge-bonded with anisotropic conductive film to a CMOS controller.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4) and U.S. manufacturability: R2R lines cost ~1% of a DRAM fab; bits per sheet are low, but 100 penny sheets could give a ~$1-2/GB capacity tier; access may sit at 100 ns-1 us rather than 10-100 ns.

title: Tier-wide back-gate plane flips cells between sprint and hibernate modes
idea: Time-multiplex the transistor threshold: each thin-film tier sits on its own buried back-gate plate, biased toward low Vt during active windows (ns to us) and swung negative during idle (seconds) to raise Vt by ~0.4 V, which cuts subthreshold leakage by ~10^4 and stretches refresh from 64 ms to seconds. It needs one plate per tier and no wiring per cell.
why: The leakage tail forces refresh (fact 3); fast access and long retention from the same cell target >10x lower refresh energy.

title: Magnify threshold during hold with FD-SOI back-gate bias
idea: Design a 1T1C or 2T cell on a 22 nm FD-SOI MPW in which the back gate swings to about -2 V during hold to raise the access transistor's Vt and cut leakage about 1000x, then returns to 0 V for fast access.
why: Refresh: retention moves from ms toward seconds on a commercial process with no new materials. Test chip and characterization cost about $400k.

title: Bond interface doubles as a shared bitline for mirrored arrays
idea: [Box: 1T1C charge | 4F2 VCT | differential cross-interface sensing | face-to-face mirror bond | Si | Cu-Cu hybrid bond] Two mirror-image VCT arrays are finished with bitline half-lines on top and bonded face-to-face so the Cu halves fuse into one bitline serving cells above and below; the sense amp compares a cell on one side with the idle half on the other, giving folded-bitline noise rejection in a 4F2 open layout.
why: Density at fixed F: two cell layers per bitline layer (2x bits per footprint), and differential sensing recovers margin lost when Cs is capped (fact 1).

title: Magnify capacitor AR to 300:1 with wet metal-assisted chemical etching
idea: Form the storage capacitor as a deep trench in the substrate using metal-assisted chemical etching, where gold or silver catalyst dots sink into Si in an HF/H2O2 bath to give AR above 300:1 with no plasma etcher. A vertical access transistor sits on top, reviving trench-capacitor DRAM.
why: Charge wall: Cs could reach about 15-20 fF at the same footprint, with a cheap wet bench instead of $50M+ high-AR plasma etchers.

title: LN2-immersed memory pods with planar 0.5 fF capacitors, 100 tiers
idea: Design for a 77 K cryogenic computer: access-transistor leakage falls ~10^6x, so retention stops sizing the capacitor and, with 64-cell short bitlines, a flat 0.5 fF planar MIM capacitor suffices, making each tier a thin planar layer and 100-tier monolithic stacks practical. Ship the memory as liquid-nitrogen-immersed CXL pods beside the accelerator (nitrogen is abundant and cheap).
why: Removes the AR 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1) and refresh (fact 3) and clears the 26+ tier break-even for 3D (fact 2) with planar tiers; claim 5-10x bits per mm2, with cooling overhead paid only on low-dissipation memory pods.

title: Chassis-body marriage: trailing U.S. logic fabs supply DRAM periphery wafers
idea: Automakers build chassis and bodies on separate lines and marry them; DRAM makers would fabricate array-only wafers and buy periphery wafers (sense amps, decoders, I/O) from U.S. 28-65 nm foundries under contract, then hybrid-bond the two.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7); offloading it frees ~40% of DRAM-fab wafer starts for arrays and creates U.S. content as a periphery-as-a-service business.

title: Bamboo-node diaphragms segment vertical lines below the Blech length
idea: Bamboo compartmentalizes its culm with periodic nodes; insert thin Ru/Co node diaphragms every ~0.5 um along vertical Cu/Mo bitlines and power pillars of tall stacks so each segment is shorter than the electromigration Blech length and atoms cannot migrate past a node.
why: 125 C electromigration in high-current vertical pillars of 100+ tier stacks: Blech-segmented lines are effectively immortal, allowing higher current density and thinner pillars (less metal, more density).

title: HP memristor sneak paths cancelled with mirrored complementary decks
idea: HPE's memristor crossbars stalled partly because sneak currents through unselected cells swamped reads in large passive arrays. Stack two decks on one shared bitline and store each bit as complementary states in the upper and lower deck. A differential read subtracts the common-mode sneak current, so selector-less arrays can grow to 4k x 4k.
why: Larger mats spread the periphery cost (fact 7) and remove selector cost, at passive 4F2 per deck. Claims array tiles ~10x larger than selector-less crossbars allow today.

title: Honeycomb: three line families at 120 degrees with active back-gate shields
idea: Forced connection to a honeycomb: put vertical-channel cells on a hex lattice with three line families at 0, 60 and 120 degrees: wordlines, bitlines, and a third family of back-gate 'shield lines'. When a wordline fires, the shield lines that cross its neighbors pulse negative to hold their channels hard off, and hex packing gives about 15% more capacitor footprint than a square grid.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and capacitor wall (fact 1): neighbors are actively clamped during aggressor activations, aiming at a ~10x flip threshold; +15% capacitor footprint per cell.

title: Packaging houses become DRAM fabs using 400 C tool sets
idea: Under 400 C, advanced-packaging and OSAT plants already run PVD, plating, ALD, steppers and hybrid bonders. They add oxide DRAM tier modules on purchased CMOS periphery wafers, with no furnaces or EUV.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: about 1/5 the capex per wafer start and uses existing U.S. packaging sites in 12-18 months.

title: Fiber-to-the-mat: photonic waveguide layer replaces TSV I/O
idea: Like fibre-to-the-home replacing copper last miles, put a silicon-nitride waveguide layer in the 3D DRAM base die with micro-ring modulators per mat cluster, carrying data at ~30 fJ/bit straight from local datalines to an off-stack optical link with no global copper datalines, TSV drivers or SerDes.
why: Data movement (facts 5, 6): ~2-3 pJ/bit of global dataline, TSV and PHY energy replaced by ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit optical path; claims ~10x lower energy per bit delivered.

title: Nanoimprint stamps print the cell layer; 180-nm steppers align everything else
idea: Scale the coin mint down to nanometers with Chou's 1995 nanoimprint: an e-beam-written master stamp, made once and cheaply replicated, presses ~15-nm hole patterns into resist for the cell layer. 180-nm KrF steppers handle the coarse periphery and straps.
why: EUV capital (fact 4): imprint tools cost ~5% of EUV, with one critical imprint per tier stack.

title: Vertical wordline makes each activation span tiers, not rows
idea: Combine tier count with page size: in a 3D array with vertical wordlines and per-tier horizontal bitlines, an activate opens one pillar's cells in all 64-128 tiers, each tier landing on its own sense amp at the staircase edge, so a page is 64-128 bits by construction.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~64-128x less activation per useful bit (activate share <0.1 pJ/bit); row hammer (fact 9): logically adjacent rows are separate pillars, not coupled neighbors.

title: Aluminum-doped zinc oxide shield planes stop vertical row-hammer coupling
idea: Insert a 5 nm ALD Al:ZnO conductive plane, grounded through the staircase, between each pair of 3D-DRAM tiers so an aggressor wordline in tier k couples into the shield instead of victim cells in tiers k+1 and k-1.
why: 3D stacking adds vertical hammer and crosstalk paths (fact 9); a grounded shield cuts inter-tier coupling ~90%, allowing tighter tier pitch without new hammer exposure, using only Al, Zn and O at 200 C.

title: Antiferroelectric-boundary dielectric biased for a giant effective permittivity
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: tune a ZrO2-rich HfZrO film to sit at its field-induced tetragonal-to-polar transition, and offset the plate voltage so the storage window rides the steep part of the P-E curve. The local dQ/dV gives k_eff ~80-120 without full ferroelectric switching.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k~70 target so a 40:1 capacitor holds what a 75:1 holds today; shorter capacitors shrink 3D tier pitch ~40%.

title: Zirconia antiferroelectric capacitors double stored charge per lateral cavity
idea: Tune ~7 nm ALD ZrO2 (thickness plus Si/Al doping) into an antiferroelectric pinched-loop state whose field-induced polar transition sits just under the 1 V storage voltage, so the capacitor releases ~2x the charge of a linear dielectric of equal area; with no remanent polarization it avoids ferroelectric fatigue.
why: Doubles effective charge per area (fact 1), letting lateral 3D capacitors be half as long and tiers thinner (fact 2), using Zr, O and Al rather than Hf or Ru.

title: Undersea-fiber draw: thermally drawn preform sliced into vertical memory arrays
idea: Fiber makers draw a macroscopic preform 100,000x into kilometers of perfectly periodic structure; assemble a centimeter preform holding a lattice of silicon cores, glass gate insulator and metal-alloy gate lines, draw it in nitrogen to ~50 nm core pitch, then slice the rod into wafers whose silicon cores become vertical channels finished by ALD. No lithography or rare gas is used for the array.
why: Array lithography and EUV capital (fact 4) eliminated; speculative ~10x lower cost per bit if drawn cores recrystallize to device grade.

title: Holographic Hadamard spreading of words across 64 tiers
idea: Revive holographic memory's trick of spreading each bit over the whole hologram: apply a Walsh-Hadamard transform across 64 tiers before writing, so 1% scattered cell errors, or one whole failed tier, become sparse errors recovered by sparse-error (compressed-sensing) decoding after the inverse transform.
why: Facts 2 and 9: tolerates tier-correlated failures and row-hammer flips without per-tier spares, letting marginal tiers ship.

title: Deposition-defined 3D DRAM patterned only with US micron-scale steppers
idea: Combine 3D NAND's thickness-defined geometry with a DRAM cell: gate length, capacitor gap and tier pitch are all set by film thickness on US-built ALD/CVD/etch tools, and the only lithography is a ~1 um hole/slit grid from US-made i-line steppers, halved by one spacer pitch split. Density comes from ~300 tiers in 3 decks and 4 cells around each hole, not from imported EUV or immersion scanners.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4) and US manufacturability: zero EUV; 0.25 um2 per hole / (4 cells x 300 tiers) is ~2e-4 um2/bit, about 4x 1-beta density.

title: Spare-tier redundancy with per-column remap fuses in bonded logic
idea: Limit: a 128-tier stack must still yield at least 95%. Build 136 tiers, test each column, and map up to eight defective tiers per column to spares through a remap table held in the bonded logic layer, replacing classic row/column sparing.
why: Fact 2: turns compound tier yield (0.995^128 = 53%) into high stack yield, making high tier counts economic.

title: Word-sized micro-mats, each with its own bond to logic
idea: Po: the page is the size of a word. Cut the array into 64x64-cell micro-mats, each with its own small sense amps and one sub-um hybrid bond straight down to the controller/compute die, so an activation opens only 64 bits and delivers all of them; millions of independent mats replace a few hundred 8 KB pages.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): 128x overfetch to ~1x, random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward <0.5 pJ per useful bit; also cuts data movement (fact 5).

title: Gearbox gate: negative-capacitance access transistor runs 0.8 V wordlines
idea: Like a gearbox multiplying torque, add a thin ferroelectric negative-capacitance layer matched to the access-transistor gate so the channel potential swings ~3x the wordline swing; drive wordlines 0-0.8 V while keeping the 13 fA off-state and drop the VPP charge pump.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline CV2 scales by (0.8/3)^2 ~ 1/14, plus ~3x pump inefficiency removed; claims >10x lower wordline energy.

title: Garage-door spring: tier back-plate bias lowers wordline swing
idea: A torsion spring carries most of a garage door's weight; give the lateral access transistors of each 3D tier a shared back-gate plate held at a retention-safe negative bias, and switch only the tier being served to a Vt-lowering bias for a batch of accesses, so front wordlines need only a ~0.9 V swing.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline energy ~ V2 drops ~11x from 3 V to 0.9 V; plate switching is amortized over hundreds of accesses per tier dwell.
